amil: تَنْصِبُ الِاسْمَ وَتَرْفَعُ الْخَبَرَ — governors that put the subject in nasb and keep the predicate in raf'

explanation.en: The six particles resembling verbs (الحروف المشبهة بالفعل): إِنَّ، أَنَّ، كَأَنَّ، لَكِنَّ، لَيْتَ، لَعَلَّ. They enter a nominal sentence and reverse كان's work: the subject (now the ism) takes nasb, the predicate (khabar) stays in raf'. In this story: إِنَّ الْعِلْمَ أَمَانَةٌ — knowledge (nasb) is a trust (raf'). Birgivi counts them among the strongest of the sixty governors; Ibn Hisham devotes a chapter of Qatr al-Nada to them.

examples.en: And people are watching you — the khabar can be a whole verbal clause.

why.en: The ism of إنّ must be mansub — learners keep the mubtada's damma out of habit.
Over-correction: only the ism takes nasb; the khabar stays marfu'. Double nasb is the classic second-stage error.
إنّ enters nominal sentences — a noun must follow it, never a verb directly.
